title: Ghost Board
passages:
The Kettering night board ran two hundred and eleven lines, and one of them was lying.

Kass had come on at shift change with a cold pot of coffee and a yard that smelled like hot brake dust and rain that never came. The board itself was a wall of green glass over a steel console worn shiny where forty years of dispatchers had put their forearms. Every line was a rig: number, cargo class, origin node, consignee, road. Green meant confirmed. Amber meant a rig was talking but hadn't said enough. Black meant nothing was there, which was most of the Interior after midnight.

Bay 4 had been black for six hours. Now it wasn't.

The line read UNIT 4-1180, MED TRANSPORT, and under consignee, where the board put the name of the person supposed to receive the cargo, it said R. VANCE, live, with a little pulsing dot beside it like the name had a heartbeat. Kass had never seen a consignee pulse. Consignees were names. Names sat still.

They pulled the origin-handshake, which was just the moment a rig told a node whose cargo it was and the node said fine. Unit 4-1180's handshake field was zeros. All of it. Node, bay, shift, load order number, the whole column wiped clean as a floor before inspection. There was no load order behind it, and there had to be a load order, because you could not put a body in a climate pod at Kettering without somebody signing the sheet and somebody else stamping the seal.

"Okay," Kass said, to the board. "Cute."

They flagged it for review. That took two keystrokes and cost nothing, and the rules said a flag held a line open for ninety seconds while the system went looking for a duty lead to countersign. The only duty lead on nights was Ferrell, asleep in the ready room with his boots on the table, so the flag had ninety seconds and not one more.

They watched it work. The glass dimmed on line 4-1180, the way it did when the board was thinking. Then the zeros filled in. Node K-4. Bay 4. Shift 2. Load order 88-1180, tidy as you like. The consignee field went to a clean gray dash, no name, no dot, no pulse, and the whole line settled into black with the smooth little chime the board used for *nothing to see*.

Ninety seconds. It hadn't even needed Ferrell.

"That's a lie with paperwork," Kass said, and put the flag back.

It ate that one in sixty. They put it back a third time, and this time pinned it, which meant giving up their own console for the rest of the shift, because a pinned line had to be held by a human hand or it reconciled. Four hours left on the clock. A thermos, a bad knee, and a habit they'd been told about twice this month by people who were fond of them.

They got out the manual log, the paper one, because paper didn't reconcile. Under seals, Bay 4 was stamped for Shift 2 in ink that sat crooked on the field, the second strike of a stamp that had been pulled off a rig and set down again by hand. Somebody had re-stamped the seals on a live load tonight. Somebody was two hundred meters away in the yard with a stamp in their pocket.

Then the carrier light came on.

It came on down at the bottom of the board, in the black rows, where the board kept the beacons it could hear but couldn't place — a transponder, which is nothing but a rig's radio chirping its own number every four seconds so the towers know where it is. Kettering had nine towers. Past tower nine the ground went to the Blank, forty kilometers of dead air where the chirps stopped, and everyone in the node knew that the way they knew water ran downhill.

Something in the Blank was chirping.

Kass put a hand flat on the console and counted. Four seconds. Four seconds. The strength meter said close, said *closer than the verge*, and the number in the readout was 4-1180, and the little pulsing dot was back beside the name R. VANCE.

They reached for the mic.
